title: Decide and record where the human session token lives
description:
**Raised 2026-09-08**, immediately after #339 shipped session persistence. Cheap to revisit now, expensive after customers exist.

---

## What shipped

#339 fixed a real defect: the workspace held the session in page memory only, so a reload looked unsigned and Google asked again. Correct fix, correctly diagnosed.

The session is now persisted in **`localStorage`** (`web/lib/auth.ts:153`):

```ts
userStore: new WebStorageStateStore({ store: window.localStorage })
```

That is the `oidc-client-ts` default and ordinary SPA practice. **This card is not "that was wrong."** It is that the tradeoff has not been examined against what this particular token authorizes.

## Why this token is not an ordinary SPA token

`localStorage` is readable by any JavaScript running on the origin. This token authorizes `PUT /turns/{turn_id}/grant` (`http/app.py:1550`, `user_router`, `RequireUserPrincipal`).

So the chain is:

**XSS on the workspace origin → read the token → grant a bot `run_terminal` → arbitrary commands on a computer running in the customer's own AWS account.**

Each link is already built and proven: `run_terminal` is on the authorization form (`chatticus-e11c17`), cross-account `RunTask` works (`chatticus-82dab7`), and the grant route is customer-facing by design.

Server-side ceiling enforcement limits this — `grant_replace_exceeds_acting_member_standing` means a stolen token cannot exceed *that member's* standing. That is real mitigation. It does not help when the stolen token belongs to an owner.

## Why the XSS precondition is not hypothetical here

This product runs an agent that **browses the web on the user's behalf**, and `docs/THREAT_MODEL.md` already treats page content as hostile (`prompt_injection_containment.feature`, "page content cannot add fields"). Any path by which fetched content, tool output, or a bot-authored message renders unescaped in the workspace is an XSS vector — and this product creates more of those paths than a typical SPA.

## The gap in the threat model

`docs/THREAT_MODEL.md` is thorough about the **agent's** browser authority — the bot holding the user's logged-in sessions, blast radius, which connectors it may touch. It says nothing about the **human's** session token, which is the credential that grants the agent its authority in the first place.

That asymmetry is worth closing regardless of which storage option is chosen.

## Options

1. **`sessionStorage`.** Meets the stated requirement — a reload in the same tab stays signed in — and is strictly narrower: not shared across tabs, cleared when the tab closes. Still XSS-readable. Costs "still signed in tomorrow", which may be a product requirement; if so, say so.
2. **httpOnly cookie / BFF.** The token never reaches JavaScript, so XSS cannot read it. Strongest, and the largest change. Worth pricing rather than dismissing, given what the token authorizes.
3. **Keep `localStorage`, deliberately.** Defensible — it is the ecosystem default. Then record it in `docs/THREAT_MODEL.md` with the compensating controls named: member-standing ceiling on grants, short token lifetime, and whatever output escaping the workspace guarantees.

Any of the three is fine. **Silence is the thing to fix.**

## Done when

`docs/THREAT_MODEL.md` records where the human session token lives, what it authorizes, and why that storage is acceptable — or the storage changes.
